excerpt: What to do first if you suspect medical malpractice in Georgia or South Carolina — records, independent care, and what not to say.
keyTakeaways: If you suspect medical malpractice, act quickly: get independent medical care, request your complete records, document everything, and avoid discussing the situation with the provider or their insurer. Georgia requires a two-year filing and expert affidavit (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71, § 9-11-9.1); South Carolina allows three years but requires a Notice of Intent to File Suit, filed together with a qualified expert's affidavit, and then mandatory mediation, before suit (S.C. Code § 15-3-545, § 15-79-125). Both states have strict statutes of repose — five years in Georgia, six in South Carolina.

faqs.question: What is the first thing I should do if I suspect medical malpractice?
faqs.answer: Seek follow-up care from a different healthcare provider immediately. An independent doctor can evaluate your condition, identify what went wrong, provide corrective treatment, and create medical records documenting the complications — all of which serve as critical evidence if you pursue a claim.

faqs.question: How do I know if what happened to me qualifies as medical malpractice?
faqs.answer: Medical malpractice occurs when a healthcare provider deviates from the accepted standard of care — doing something a competent provider would not have done, or failing to do something they should have — and that deviation causes harm. A bad outcome alone is not malpractice. A medical malpractice attorney can review your records and consult with medical experts to determine whether your case qualifies.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a medical malpractice lawsuit in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Georgia imposes a two-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71) from the date the injury occurred. There is no general discovery rule: only a foreign object left in the body gets one year from discovery (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-72). An absolute five-year statute of repose applies. Georgia also requires an expert affidavit at the time of filing (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-9.1).

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a medical malpractice lawsuit in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: South Carolina allows three years from the date of the negligent act or from discovery (S.C. Code § 15-3-545), with a six-year statute of repose. Before suing, you must also file a Notice of Intent to File Suit together with a qualified expert's affidavit, and serve it on each defendant, which tolls the deadline; the parties must then mediate before the lawsuit can be filed (S.C. Code §§ 15-79-125, 15-36-100).

faqs.question: Should I talk to my doctor or the hospital about the suspected malpractice?
faqs.answer: No. Do not confront the provider, give a recorded statement to their malpractice insurer, or sign any documents without having an attorney review them first. Anything you say can be documented and used against you. Once you hire an attorney, all communications go through your legal team.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to hire a medical malpractice attorney?
faqs.answer: Most medical malpractice attorneys work on a contingency fee basis, meaning you pay nothing upfront and owe nothing unless your case results in compensation. The attorney advances all costs of investigation, expert review, and litigation. This makes experienced legal representation accessible regardless of your financial situation.
